contempt

kun-TEMPT — rhymes with 'attempt'; contempt attempts no respect at all. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Contempt is a feeling that someone or something deserves scorn or is beneath respect.

The senator's contempt for the reporters' questions was obvious from his dismissive tone.

Example

A judge listens to a witness lie under oath, repeatedly and shamelessly, even after being caught. Her expression hardens into open contempt, and she refuses to look at the witness for the rest of the hearing.

She feels a total lack of respect for someone she now considers dishonest and worthless. Unlike 'anger,' which is a hot, active emotion, contempt is a cold, dismissive sense that someone doesn't even deserve a reaction.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

scorn: Scorn is contempt let out into the open — a sneer, a cutting remark, a public brush-off. Contempt is the feeling underneath, and it can stay hidden behind a polite face for years. If the disrespect is being shown, call it scorn; if it is only felt, it is contempt.

disdain: Disdain is the feeling that someone or something is unworthy of your attention — a cool superiority that mostly looks away. Contempt is harsher: it adds the judgment that its target deserves scorn, not just a shrug. Disdain turns its nose up; contempt condemns.

derision: Derision is contemptuous ridicule or mockery said or shown out loud — laughter, jeers, cutting imitations. Contempt is the silent judgment behind it: you can hold someone in contempt for years without saying a word, but derision only exists once the mockery is expressed.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

admiration: respect and warm approval

reverence: deep, awed respect

Where it sits · how deep the scorn runs — dislike → contempt → loathing

dislike vs. contempt: Dislike is weaker than contempt — you can dislike something without judging it as worthless, while contempt adds that cold sense that it doesn't even deserve respect.

loathing vs. contempt: Loathing is stronger than contempt: contempt is a cold, dismissive judgment, but loathing is a hot, intense revulsion.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — con- (com-)

prefix — con- (com-): intensive (Latin)

root — -tempt- (-temn-)

root — -tempt- (-temn-): to scorn, to despise (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin contemnere meant 'to scorn utterly.' Contempt is that same feeling — treating someone or something as beneath notice or worthless.

Use the root in a new word: contemptible

Use the root in a new word: contemptible: 'Contemptible,' the coach said quietly, and refused to discuss the matter any further.
